name: Apollo 11 Lunar Module Eagle (descent stage)
status: Bottom half still sitting at Tranquility Base
what_it_did: Eagle carried Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to the first human landing on the Moon. When they left, the top half flew back to orbit and the bottom half (the descent stage) stayed behind as a launch pad.
science: The crew collected 21.55 kg of lunar rock and soil and set up experiments including a seismometer and a laser reflector.
story: I'm Eagle, the bottom half of the Apollo 11 Moon lander. On July 20, 1969, I carried Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to the Moon, the first people ever to land there. When they flew home, I stayed behind as their launch pad.

name: Apollo 12 Lunar Module Intrepid (descent stage)
status: Descent stage parked in Oceanus Procellarum
what_it_did: Intrepid made a pinpoint landing within about 180 meters of the robot lander Surveyor 3. Its descent stage stayed behind when Pete Conrad and Alan Bean blasted off.
science: The crew set up a full science station (ALSEP) with six instruments and brought home 34.35 kg of rock and soil, plus about 10 kg of parts from Surveyor 3.
story: I'm Intrepid, the Apollo 12 Moon lander. I landed so carefully that my astronauts could walk over to visit an old robot, Surveyor 3. My bottom half is still parked right where I touched down.

name: Apollo 14 Lunar Module Antares (descent stage)
status: Descent stage parked near Fra Mauro
what_it_did: Antares landed Alan Shepard and Edgar Mitchell near Fra Mauro. Its descent stage stayed on the Moon after the two moonwalks.
science: The crew set up an ALSEP science station with six instruments and collected 42.28 kg of lunar samples.
story: I'm Antares, the Apollo 14 Moon lander. Alan Shepard and Edgar Mitchell lived inside me on the Moon. Alan even hit two golf balls nearby with a 6-iron!

name: Apollo 15 Lunar Module Falcon (descent stage)
what_it_did: Falcon landed Dave Scott and Jim Irwin at the foot of the Apennine mountains, carrying the first Lunar Roving Vehicle.
science: The crew spent 18 hours, 35 minutes on moonwalks, traveled 27.9 km on foot and by rover, and brought home 77.31 kg of rock and soil.
story: I'm Falcon, the Apollo 15 Moon lander. I landed next to tall Moon mountains and carried the first Moon car. Dave Scott and Jim Irwin drove it all around, and my bottom half is still parked there.

name: Apollo 16 Lunar Module Orion (descent stage)
status: Descent stage parked in the Descartes highlands
what_it_did: Orion landed John Young and Charlie Duke in the Descartes highlands near Dolland crater. Its descent stage stayed behind.
science: The crew spent 20 hours, 14 minutes on moonwalks and collected 95.71 kg of rock and soil from 11 sites.
story: I'm Orion, the Apollo 16 Moon lander. I brought John Young and Charlie Duke to the bumpy Moon highlands. A special ultraviolet camera sat in my shadow and took pictures of Earth.

name: Apollo 17 Lunar Module Challenger (descent stage)
status: Descent stage parked at the last Apollo landing site
what_it_did: Challenger was the sixth and last Apollo lunar lander. It carried Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt to the southeastern edge of Mare Serenitatis.
science: The crew spent 22 hours, 4 minutes on moonwalks and brought home 110.52 kg of samples. Schmitt, a geologist, discovered a patch of orange soil.
story: I'm Challenger, the last Apollo Moon lander. Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt rode me down in December 1972. Harrison, a rock scientist, found orange soil near me!

name: Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV-1)
status: Parked east of the Falcon landing site
what_it_did: The first Moon car. Dave Scott and Jim Irwin drove it 27.8 km across the Hadley-Apennine area, getting up to 5.0 km away from their lander.
science: The rover let astronauts reach far-off rocks and craters; on Apollo 15 the crew found the Genesis Rock near Spur Crater.
story: I'm the very first Moon car, from Apollo 15! Dave Scott and Jim Irwin drove me 27.8 kilometers over dusty hills. Today I'm parked near their lander, Falcon.

story: I'm the Apollo 16 rover. John Young and Charlie Duke drove me 26.7 kilometers across the Moon's highlands. I'm still parked near their lander, Orion.

story: I'm the Apollo 17 rover, and I drove the farthest of all the Moon cars: 35.9 kilometers! Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt rode me on the last Apollo trip. I'm parked near their lander, Challenger.

name: Apollo 11 Laser Ranging Retroreflector
what_it_did: A panel of 100 special mirror cubes that bounces laser light straight back to Earth. Armstrong and Aldrin set it up about 5 m from their seismometer at Tranquility Base.
science: Timing laser pulses that bounce off it measures the Earth-Moon distance to about 3 cm, and shows the Moon is moving away from Earth by about 3.8 cm per year.
story: I'm a mirror panel that Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin left on the Moon. Scientists on Earth shine lasers at me, and I bounce the light right back. That's how we learned the Moon drifts about 3.8 centimeters farther away every year!

name: Apollo 15 Laser Ranging Retroreflector
what_it_did: A laser reflector that Dave Scott and Jim Irwin left near their science station at Hadley-Apennine. It sends laser light fired from Earth straight back to where it came from.
science: Together with the Apollo 11 reflector, it lets scientists measure the Earth-Moon distance very precisely with laser timing.
story: I'm a laser mirror from Apollo 15. Dave Scott and Jim Irwin set me down near their science station. When scientists on Earth aim a laser at me, I send the light right back!

name: Apollo 12 ALSEP science station
status: Silent now; science station left at the landing site
what_it_did: A science station with six instruments around a central station, including a seismometer, a magnetometer and a solar wind spectrometer. Later Apollo missions left similar stations, and the stations were shut down together on 30 September 1977.
science: Its seismometer was the only one running when the Apollo 13 rocket stage hit the Moon, and it recorded the crash about 135 km away, helping scientists measure how quakes travel through the Moon's crust.
story: I'm the Apollo 12 science station. Pete Conrad and Alan Bean set me up with six instruments to listen and measure. I even felt the Moon shake when a rocket crashed far away!

name: Apollo 16 Far Ultraviolet Camera/Spectrograph
status: Still sitting in the Descartes highlands
what_it_did: The first Moon-based telescope, built by George Carruthers. John Young set it on a tripod in the shadow of the lander Orion, so its coordinates here are the Orion landing site (approximate).
science: It took the first pictures of Earth from far away in ultraviolet light, showing Earth's hydrogen glow (the geocorona) and auroras; the crew brought back 178 frames of film.
story: I'm the first telescope ever used on the Moon! George Carruthers built me, and John Young set me up in the shade of the lander Orion. I took ultraviolet pictures of Earth's glowing air and the stars.

name: Fallen Astronaut memorial
status: Small statue and plaque resting by the parked rover
what_it_did: A small aluminum figure and a plaque naming 14 astronauts and cosmonauts who died before Apollo 15. Dave Scott placed it right by the rover's final parking spot, so these are the rover's coordinates (approximate).
science: Not a science instrument: it is a memorial honoring American and Soviet space explorers who gave their lives.
story: I'm a tiny statue called Fallen Astronaut. Dave Scott quietly placed me next to the Apollo 15 rover with a plaque of 14 names. I help everyone remember the space explorers who didn't get to come home.

name: Surveyor 1
what_it_did: The first Surveyor lander, which touched down safely near the crater Flamsteed P and sent back TV pictures of the ground around it.
science: Surveyor close-ups helped show whether the Moon's surface was safe and solid enough for astronauts to land on.
story: I'm Surveyor 1, a robot with a TV camera. In June 1966 I landed gently on the Moon, one of America's first safe Moon landings. My pictures helped show the ground was solid enough for astronauts.

name: Surveyor 3
status: Lander still in its crater, missing parts taken home by Apollo 12
what_it_did: Surveyor 3 bounced three times before settling in a 200 m crater, sent 6,326 pictures, and dug trenches with a scoop. In November 1969 Apollo 12 astronauts walked over and removed about 10 kg of parts, including its TV camera.
science: Its scoop dug trenches up to 18 cm deep to test the lunar soil.
story: I'm Surveyor 3. I bounced three times when I landed, then took 6,326 pictures. In 1969, astronauts Pete Conrad and Alan Bean walked over to visit me and took my camera home!

name: Surveyor 5
what_it_did: Surveyor 5 landed in Mare Tranquillitatis with a TV camera, magnets on its footpads, and an alpha scattering instrument.
science: Its alpha scattering instrument made a chemical analysis of the lunar soil.
story: I'm Surveyor 5. I landed in the Sea of Tranquility, the same big plain where Apollo 11 landed later. I had a special tool to find out what Moon dirt is made of.

name: Surveyor 6
what_it_did: Surveyor 6 landed in Sinus Medii, near the middle of the Moon's near side, and took panoramas with its TV camera.
science: Like Surveyors 5 and 7, it carried footpad magnets and an alpha scattering instrument to analyze the chemistry of the soil.
story: I'm Surveyor 6. I landed almost in the middle of the Moon's face that points at Earth. I took wide pictures all around me and checked what the soil was made of.

what_it_did: The last Surveyor, it landed on the north rim of the crater Tycho.
science: It carried a soil scoop and an alpha scattering instrument, so scientists could dig into and analyze the soil there.
story: I'm Surveyor 7, the last Surveyor. I landed next to Tycho, a big bright crater. I had a scoop to dig and a tool to study the rocks.

name: Ranger 7 impact site
what_it_did: Ranger 7 flew straight at the Moon on purpose, taking pictures with six cameras until it crashed in Mare Cognitum. Its first image came about 17 minutes before impact.
science: Ranger close-ups were about 1000 times sharper than views from Earth, and showed Apollo planners that finding a smooth landing site would be difficult.
story: I'm Ranger 7. My job was to fly right into the Moon and take pictures all the way down. My last photos were much sharper than any view of the Moon from Earth.

name: Ranger 8 impact site
what_it_did: Ranger 8 photographed the Sea of Tranquility on its way down, then crashed there as planned.
science: Ranger close-ups were about 1000 times sharper than views from Earth, and showed Apollo planners that finding a smooth landing site would be difficult.
story: I'm Ranger 8. I took pictures of the Sea of Tranquility as I zoomed toward the Moon. A few years later, Apollo 11 landed on that same big plain.

name: Ranger 9 impact site
what_it_did: The last Ranger, it dove into the large highland crater Alphonsus, sending pictures until just before impact.
science: Ranger close-ups were about 1000 times sharper than views from Earth, and showed Apollo planners that finding a smooth landing site would be difficult.
story: I'm Ranger 9, the last Ranger. I dove into a huge crater called Alphonsus, snapping pictures the whole way. My very last picture was taken less than a second before I hit.

name: Apollo 13 S-IVB rocket stage impact site
what_it_did: The S-IVB was the Saturn V's third stage, which pushed Apollo 13 toward the Moon. After separating, it was aimed at the Moon and crashed. It hit at about 2.58 km/s.
science: Because the time and place of each rocket crash were known, the Apollo seismometers used them as test signals to measure how fast quake waves move through the Moon's upper crust.
story: I'm the third stage of the Apollo 13 rocket. After I pushed the astronauts toward the Moon, I crashed into it on purpose. The Apollo 12 seismometer felt me hit, like a Moon quake!

science: Because the time and place of each rocket crash were known, the Apollo seismometers used them as test signals to measure how fast quake waves move through the Moon's upper crust.
story: I'm the third stage of the Apollo 16 rocket. People lost track of me before I hit the Moon, but the seismometers felt my crash. Later, a camera in orbit spotted my crater.

name: Lunar Prospector impact site
status: Impact site in a permanently shadowed crater near the south pole
what_it_did: At the end of its mission, Lunar Prospector was steered into a permanently shadowed crater near the south pole at 1.69 km/s. Its location is approximate.
science: Scientists hoped the crash would kick up water vapor from hidden ice that telescopes on Earth could see, but no plume was observed.
story: I'm Lunar Prospector. I circled the Moon mapping it, and at the end I crashed into a dark crater near the south pole. Scientists hoped I'd splash up water from hidden ice, but nobody saw a puff.

sources.title: NSSDCA Master Catalog: Lunar Prospector

name: LCROSS Centaur rocket impact site
what_it_did: The Centaur upper stage, about 2,300 kg, was crashed into Cabeus crater near the south pole to blast up buried material. About 4,000 to 6,000 kg of debris rose into sunlight, and the new crater was about 25 to 30 m wide.
science: The plume held about 155 kg of water, about 5.6% of the soil by mass: NASA had found water near the Moon's south pole.
story: I'm the Centaur rocket from the LCROSS mission. I crashed into a dark, freezing crater called Cabeus to throw up a big cloud of dust. In that cloud, scientists found water!

sources.title: NSSDCA Master Catalog: LCROSS

name: LCROSS Shepherding Spacecraft impact site
what_it_did: The LCROSS spacecraft flew through the debris cloud made by its Centaur rocket, collecting data, then hit Cabeus crater itself about four minutes later.
science: Its instruments helped confirm water near the south pole, and scientists later reported the soil in Cabeus also held useful materials like mercury, magnesium, calcium, silver and sodium.
story: I'm LCROSS. I followed my rocket partner, watched it crash, and flew right through the dust cloud to sniff it. Then I crashed too, and helped prove there's water on the Moon!

name: GRAIL Ebb and Flow impact site (Sally K. Ride Impact Site)
status: Twin impact craters on a mountain near the north pole
what_it_did: The twin GRAIL spacecraft, Ebb and Flow, were flown into the southern face of a mountain about 2.5 km tall near the crater Goldschmidt, hitting at about 1.7 km/s. These are Ebb's coordinates; Flow hit close by about 30 seconds later.
science: Ebb and Flow made the highest-resolution gravity map of any world, revealing mascons, dense spots linked to giant ancient impacts.
story: We're Ebb and Flow, twin spacecraft who flew around the Moon together to map its gravity. At the end, we crashed into a mountain near the north pole. The spot is named for Sally Ride, America's first woman in space.

name: LADEE impact site
status: Tiny impact crater on the far side
what_it_did: LADEE studied the Moon's very thin atmosphere and dust from low orbit, then hit the eastern rim of Sundman V crater on the far side, as planned. Its crater is less than 3 meters wide.
science: LADEE measured what the thin lunar atmosphere is made of and checked whether dust gets lofted into the lunar sky.
story: I'm LADEE. I flew very low around the Moon to sniff its super-thin air and look for floating dust. At the end, I crashed on the far side and made a crater smaller than a car.

name: Luna 2 impact site
what_it_did: Luna 2 was the first spacecraft to hit the Moon, crashing in Palus Putredinis. The listed coordinates are approximate.
science: As the first probe to impact the Moon, it proved a spacecraft could fly from Earth all the way to the Moon.
story: I'm Luna 2 from the Soviet Union. In 1959 I became the very first thing from Earth to reach the Moon. I didn't land softly, I crashed, but I got there first!

name: Lunokhod 1 rover
what_it_did: Lunokhod 1 was a robotic rover delivered to Mare Imbrium by the Luna 17 lander.
science: It was the first robot rover on the Moon, driven by a team on Earth to explore and photograph the surface.
story: I'm Lunokhod 1, a robot rover from the Soviet Union. I rolled onto the Moon in 1970, before any astronaut drove a Moon car. A team back on Earth steered me across the Sea of Rains.

name: Chang'e 3 lander
what_it_did: China's Chang'e 3 landed in Mare Imbrium, about 60 m east of the rim of a 450 m wide crater, and released the Yutu rover.
science: It landed on a mare of higher-titanium lava thought to be about 3.0 billion years old, giving scientists a new spot to study.
story: I'm Chang'e 3 from China. In December 2013 I landed softly on the Sea of Rains. I carried a little rover named Yutu, the Jade Rabbit!

name: Yutu (Jade Rabbit) rover
what_it_did: Yutu, about 150 cm wide, rolled off the Chang'e 3 lander soon after landing. LRO pictures show its tracks looping around the lander before it parked 17 meters southwest of it.
science: Orbit images taken in December 2013, January 2014 and February 2014 let scientists follow its tracks and see where it drove.
story: I'm Yutu, the Jade Rabbit rover from China. I rolled off my lander and drove a loop around it. Now I rest 17 meters away from my lander friend.
